## The prose

The Qitaf smelled of singed rope and sea-sour musk, and Port Aden kept its usual throb of hawkers and cartwheels like a fever under everything. We had come in on a tide that rinsed the docks with blood-salty water and the taste of copper still clung to my tongue; the raid's clatter had not yet left my bones. I remember the way the dawn threw the city's awnings into hard relief, the way a gull made a single, obscene call and then was gone. I remember, too, the quiet on my ship—the kind that settles after you pull a job clean and your crew counts what they kept and what they lost.

I was on the Qitaf, tied to Port Aden's eastern quay. My boots left salt on the planks; Rasim, who never quite believed the sea would swallow him, was on the helm like a prayer, hands grafted to the tiller. Yusuf moved through the deck with the slow certainty of an old watch spring—checking lines, looking at faces. He was the measure against my recklessness; when I looked at him I could tell how badly the last run had bitten us.

We had hauled in two chests and a war-standard that would fetch half a market; we had taken candy from a governor's store-room and a knife that reminded me of my father's hand. There were groans down below and the smell of vinegar on a seamstress's bundle; Port Aden would hum another story by noon. I had meant to drink, to count, and to let the crew stray into the market until we could put distance between ourselves and the smell of hot iron.

Instead, a shadow stepped onto our gangway.

He did not belong to the port or to the sea. Azraq moved as if corners were courtesy he did not need; the hem of his robe skimmed the planks without a single salt flake. His eyes were not a sailor's—silver and sharp, like weatherglass. The crew fell quiet because they always fall quiet for what they cannot name. He carried two small things: a paper, dark with salt and thumb-smear, and a folded folio that looked as if it had bled through with other men's maps.

He did not make a grand entrance. He set the papers on a crate between the hammocks and let them be seen. His voice was cool enough to make the smoke of our brazier duck away.

"I am Azraq," he said—not the elaborate Peri titles you read in the old stories, just the one word, a thing delivered and firm. "The Peri Council sent me."

Names have weight; they are knots you can neither unknot nor tie unless you have the rope. Azraq did not hand me a rope. He offered me, instead, a condition.

He drew the torn log up from the folio and spread it with a thumb that left a smudge of dark salt. The paper was thick with other people's panic—ink run into the weave, a diagram scratched out and half-smudged. The map sat folded like a sleeping thing: margins full of notes in different hands, a coastline recast and rescored. I watched the crew lean toward those two objects the way people lean toward a strange illness—curious, afraid for their reasons.

He used the papers as proof. He did not read them to us the way a judge reads a will; he let us see the smears and the lines. He said, simply, that they had been pulled from a wreck near Isle Jarrah, that they told of a loom at the island's heart and a thing that turns threads into fate. I listened with a captain's half-skepticism and a thief's hunger. How much had been survived, how much had been invented between desperate hands and salt—those were questions for later. For the moment, the papers were enough.

"We require a mortal to do what we will not," Azraq said. "You will take a single thing."

There was no theatrical flourish when he named it. He gave the mission like a nail: precise, inevitable.

He named my task: "steal the spindle from Isle Jarrah."

Uproar is a poor word for the way noise re-entered the Qitaf. Yusuf's fingers tightened on the rail until the bone showed. Rasim's face lost the color it had clung to. The crew exchanged looks like sailors reading water. To take something from an island that men whispered about and then never left—this was not a job, it was a sentence.

"The Peri Council has no notion of risk the way we do," Azraq added. There was no plea in it, no apology; the permanence in his tone made the very timbers under our feet feel less stubborn. "We do not bargain with time. We cannot thread this ourselves. That is where you come in."

Yusuf stepped forward. He does not show fear the way a child does; his fear is practical. "And if we refuse?" His voice cut like a reef.

Azraq tilted his head, as if considering a trinket. "Refusal will be answered," he said. "But there is a means to accept."

He lifted the smaller thing, a pendant set with silver-blue glass, rimmed like a choked moon. He did not explain its making—peri law does not translate into our markets—but he took the amulet to me as if it were an invoice.

He closed the amulet at my throat.

It sank like cold coin into my skin and the world learned to care about obedience. There was a sharp, concrete pain, the precise metallic bite of something that knows the shape of oaths. For a moment I felt my hands not as my own but as if someone else had balanced them in the air and were weighing their capacity to harm. My wrists tightened instinctively; the amulet hummed once, a thin sound like a gull's wing against rope.

"You will do what you are told," Azraq said. "You will not leave your charge."

I found my mouth and managed a laugh that came out dry. "And if I—"

When I tried to wrench it free, a hot spike flared under my ribs and something deep and old drew a line through my head. The pain was a command in another language. It did not merely hurt; it argued. My knees folded a hair. I swallowed so hard I tasted iron.

Yusuf caught my arm. His face was an animal map of all the memos and debts that had led us here. "You right with that thing on you?" he asked, not angry so much as calculating. "You right with them sending their teeth to us?"

Azraq's gaze slid to him like a blade checking for purchase. "It is binding," he said. "It will enforce compliance. Resistance will be costly. If you succeed, the Council's terms will be as they are stated."

I had never been a woman to bow to the things that wanted what mortals have. I had grown used to measuring threats with the edges of knives and the clarity of a gun's barrel. This was not like that. This was a law glued to my throat.

The papers remained on the crate between the hammocks. They were not offered as payment and they were not tucked away. They stayed there while we argued, a small, steady ruin of someone else's fate. I touched the folio without thinking and salt skin roughened my thumb.

In the end, it was not bravery or thirst for legend that bent me. It was the arithmetic of the crew. Yusuf's jaw is a map of our ledger; when he decides something is worth paying for, he knows the price by the way men will sleep. I thought of Rasim, hands clinging to a wheel that had carried us through storms that did not care what gods watched. I thought of the groans below that told me someone had hurt in the raid but would live, and I thought of the city, of the markets and the mothers who had nothing.

"We go for the spindle," I said finally. My voice sounded like a rope dragged over wood—frayed, too loud. "But we go my way as much as I can make it so. I keep my crew. You keep your interest hands off while I'm on her."

Azraq's mouth tightened the fraction it needed. The silver in his eyes did not change. "You keep your crew, within the terms we set," he said. "The Council watches."

So it began: a stolen morning at Port Aden, a binding at my throat, a scrap of paper and a folded map on a crate like a promise I had not asked for. The Qitaf rocked in her berth as if testing the sea's patience. The harbor lay open and indifferent. I tasted copper and obligation, and the world felt both smaller and vaster at once.

The mission's wording "steal the spindle from Isle Jarrah" is used verbatim as required. I have described the amulet's sensation but have not invented an activation ritual.

I had not expected to find the answer to an immortal's patience in the thin scrape of a fingernail. Azraq had sat on my crate like an accusation, and when the light hit the silver at his throat it made the boards look cheap. He spoke without hurry, as if explaining the weather, but everything in the room tightened to hear him.

He uncapped nothing; he only unfolded the map again, letting the paper look ragged and earnest in the brazier's glow. "The Council wants one thing," he said. His voice was small enough to be cruel. "A single spindle."

He said the word and let it sit between us. I had heard it before—the mission phrased out of the wreck-map that had bled into the folio a day earlier—but the second time it landed differently, like a nettle placed on the palm. "The Spindle," I repeated, because names were the handles you used on troubles. "From Isle Jarrah."

He nodded. "Isle Jarrah. The island with its own rules. The witches' work is there. We cannot—must not—enter their loom. We require a mortal hand."

Here was the part I had expected and the part I had not. The expected was the terse clarity of what they wanted; the unexpected was how little else he would say. He explained that the Peri Council had reasons; he would not make them mine. "Our reasons are not for your keeping," he said. "They are urgent. You must understand urgency without understanding why."

I had been a woman who measured bargains in coin and in the lives that coin bought. Urgency dressed up as a fact would not have moved me on its own. But urgency said aloud by a Peri did not feel like a fact so much as a law: it bent the air.

"And if we refuse?" Yusuf asked. His voice had the bluntness of a man who preferred problems with edges. He did not ask aloud what I had already been thinking—the kind of avarice that asked whether you could sell your life cheap and still sleep—but he wanted to know the shape of the answer.

Azraq's hands, pale as bone, did not tremble. "Refusal will be answered," he said. He did not explain the answer. He let the silence do the rest. "It will be answered by covenant. By consequence. By measures that make refusal a worse balance than acceptance."

The words did not tell me what that balance was. They were a promise of consequence and nothing more. That was a kind of threat the sea understood by smell, and I remembered the look on Rasim's face when I first told him we chased storms for work.

I had started to ask whether "answered" meant exile, or curses on cargo, or worse. Instead, I reached for the amulet at my throat like a woman checking a burn. The silver-blue glass sat cold on my skin where Azraq had locked it shut. When I thought about prying it loose, a quick, hot thing stabbed under my ribs as if someone had found the seam of me and slackened it.

Pain was a blunt instrument. It did more than fold my hands for a moment; it argued a law into my head. My fingers went clumsy, like a man who had his tools taken away, and the room reeled for a breath.

Azraq watched me with that same thin patience. "It is binding," he said. "It enforces compliance. Resistance is costly."

I tried to make a joke because anger liked air, but the amulet's tug made my laugh break in half. "And unbinding?" I asked. "Is there a way round a peri's glue?"

He leaned forward then, the only movement that suggested interest. "Not none. Not absolute. The instrument we affix is a law, not a god. It can be resisted by a strong mortal will, it can be countered by the witches' craft, and it can be made irrelevant by what you seek—the Spindle—if used under the island's terms."

Those three things landed like possible exits: will, witchcraft, the Spindle. I imagined the dark needle of the spindle altering the stitch that had closed my throat and the idea made my mouth dry. The Peri had just named the tools that could unmake their leash. That was information. It changed the shape of my anger into a kind of calculation.

"You cannot do what you ask because you are unwilling," Azraq said at last, answering a question he had not been asked. "Not because you lack hands. The Council cannot thread the island's craft without breaking its own laws. That is why you, a mortal with a ship and crew, are the instrument."

There was still more he would not say. He would not speak of what the Peri would gain, only that it was necessary and not the kind of necessity it would be polite to explain. The opacity of it was part of their power; they could claim moral distance by refusing to name the ends.

I thought of the crew below, of Yusuf's slow, ledgered calculations, of Rasim's hands on the wheel and the small jokes he hid in the ropes. I thought of the groans that had come up from the hold after the raid and the men who would not wake if I sold them some dangerous notion of freedom for a better future. The amulet bit a second time when my thought bent toward a way out that involved walking away; the spike had a memory like a compass—that if I pulled from a binding, the bond would remind me why it had been there.

"You want me to go," I said. Saying it made the word solid. "You want the Spindle from Isle Jarrah. You have bound me to that task. I will go. But I go to keep my crew. I keep my command. Your enforcement stays on my throat, but your hands stay out of my ship while she is mine."

Azraq's silver eyes did not soften, but the two corners of his mouth shifted the littlest. "You keep them, within the terms the Council sets," he said. "And you will deliver."

That was the turn: a knife of acceptance and the rust on its blade. I had not been proud of every bargain I had struck in my years, but I had kept my promise to the men who sailed under me, and I had meant to keep this one. The room smelled of boiled coffee and tar; the map looked like someone else's dying hope, a thing neither dead nor alive. Azraq folded the folio back into itself and let it go.

When he left, the amulet hummed once against my skin—a small, private sound. It was not a scream, nor was it a benediction. It was a machine setting itself to work.

I had a map, a crew, and a binding on my throat. I had also, now, a sliver of knowledge: that the very thing the Council wanted might also be the thing that could make the Council's hold useless. That thought was a weight and a blade both.

The deck smelled of tar and coffee; the city behind us was a low, confused thing of smoke and market cries. I was on the Qitaf's deck when I called them up. The map lay between us, its paper thin and folded into a shape that had learned to be useful. The folio's edges were soft with handling; I spread the battered folio-map on the hatch and ran my thumb along the smudged coastline until the shapes in it stopped looking like geography and started looking like a problem I could hold.

They came in groups of two or three, dragging sleep out of their faces and the crawl of the hold from their joints. I did not call them to frighten them; I called them because truths are worse when they are hidden and because the thing at my throat did not belong in the dark. Yusuf was there by the mast, his palms white on the rail. There are men who become the ledger of a ship, and Yusuf had always been more of a balance than a book—he did not leap, he measured.

I told them what Azraq had said. I called the crew up and told them what Azraq had said: we were bound to fetch the Spindle from Isle Jarrah. I watched their faces in the wavering lantern-light—some went slack, some hard, the rest a kind of knitting together of fear and appetite. "Isle Jarrah," someone muttered, as if naming the island would make it less a sentence.

The amulet at my throat hummed once against my skin and stung when I let my thoughts stray to walking away. I had accepted the mission because the amulet made saying no a luxury I could not buy. Saying it aloud did not make it smaller; it only moved the feeling into a place where I could see its edges.

Yusuf folded his arms, jaw set. "We keep the ship," he said, the words flat as a bilge plank. "We don't throw her away for someone else's war."

He did not say it like a question. He said it like a condition. I wanted to argue, to fling some heroic image into the air and make them believe it was a choice I had chosen. That was not the truth tonight. The truth was nearer and colder: a Peri had fastened metal and law to my throat and called it duty.

So we argued the numbers without numbers. I talked about what losing the Qitaf would mean in stories, and Yusuf answered with the city-side of things—medicine for Rasim's cough when it came, a replacement rope when the last raid frayed the old, a chef's pay for the men so the cooking stayed decent. Our conversation was arithmetic without sums; we used the words of risk instead of figures because the figures were ours and private. I made them count what mattered in boats: bread, repair, warm beds for the winter. "We are worth more intact than a spindle is worth to a council who will not look us in the eye," Yusuf said. It was not bravado. It was prudence.

I told them plainly: I keep the Qitaf and my command. I will not send them to a death she did not need to take. I had told Azraq's envoy that his agents would keep their hands off the ship while she was mine. I meant it. Saying it did not change the binding at my throat, but it shaped what I could bargain away and what I could not.

They watched me say it. Saying a thing to a man is different from swearing it to a god; men can hold you to what you said. I wanted them to anchor to that sentence so none of us could drift into an excuse later.

Still, the amulet made itself remembered. Every time the thought of leaving to save my own skin uncoiled, a hot pricking woke along my ribs. It was a small tyranny, mechanical and exact. Pain is tidy that way. It made the choice a calculation: I would go because my throat was given no good alternative.

There was a softer, fiercer promise under the calculation. "If we do this," I said, and the map's paper scraped under my palm, "we do it because we have to, and because we will do it in a way that keeps what cannot be replaced. We bring the Spindle back if it lets us, but not at the cost of the Qitaf. Not at the cost of you lot down there."

A low laugh came from the cockroach of a man who had been in the mizzen the night the roof of a warehouse had caved. It was not brave. It was the familiarity of people who knew their captain's softness as well as her stubbornness. Yusuf nodded once.

Preparations followed talk as obediently as tides follow the moon. We made the Qitaf ready to go: canvas lashed, lines checked, the hold stowed. Lanterns were trimmed and hung where they would not blow out, the bilge was run, the anchor's windlass oiled. Men I had not named by name moved with the certainty of people who have done the same routine a hundred times and know every error by heart. I handed the folio back to Yusuf and said, "Keep a copy of where we think the reefs lie. We'll trust nothing we are not ready to forgive when it bites." He folded the map and kept it under his arm like a thing to be guarded.

Before we dropped the last of the ropes I ran my fingers over the silver-blue glass at my throat. The amulet was patient as a storm and as indifferent. It would not be reasoned into forgetting. It would only be moved by the two things Azraq had named: the witches' craft or the Spindle itself. That was a future I could not yet buy, but it was a road we had to walk.

We cast off at a time that was not proud nor theatrical; there was no trumpeting. The Qitaf slid from the berth with the mild indignity of something who did the same thing every day and had learned to be graceful about it. The city fell behind, thin as a breath, and I kept watch on the horizon with the worn map between my knees. I had a crew who knew what they had signed up for and a binding at my throat that would remind me of the price of answering a Peri's call.

The market smelled of sun-baked spice and old tar; men shouted over yards of cloth and the bellows of the fishmongers spat a salt that hung on the back of my throat. I moved through it like a woman counting coins she meant to spend—quick hands, brief smiles, a face that said business and nothing more. We could not afford vanity in our purchases. We could afford only what would keep hull and hand from failing us at sea.

I bought oil that wouldn't blacken the wicks in a storm, wax to bed the seams, a coil of good line that felt like it might outlive a man's patience, and a wrapped bundle of bitter herbs the apothecary said would steady a coughing chest. The herbs were for Rasim, because Yusuf had said last night, flat and clean, that if we lost the Qitaf then Rasim's cough would go without a salve and the rest of us would sleep on harder things. I kept my hand on the coins until the merchant's fingers were closed, then let the night swallow the small trade and the change.

When I came back to the ship the deck smelled different—sea and tar and the up-throb of men waiting for a rhythm—and the folio lay open on the hatch like a private thing left unattended. Yusuf was already there, sleeves hitched, the map loosened between his palms as if he were balancing a thought.

They came in twos and threes, blinking the market dust from their eyes. Rasim pulled his coat tighter and coughed once as he took the top step, like a man testing whether he could keep standing if the world decided to press on him. A handful of faces leaned over the paper while lantern-light pooled on its folded edge.

We'd already argued the numbers; there was nothing to be gained by saying them again. The map and the log were what we had instead: paper that whispered of mistakes people had left behind. The folio had been handled so much that the coastline had gone soft where hands had smudged it; there were crosses darkened into blurs and pencil lines that started with confidence and ended in a scrawl. It suggested navigation rather than instructions—finger-thin errors sketched in ink, not the sort of handwriting you followed without a rope and a prayer.

A man—one I had seen at the mizzen, his face a shadowed thing—leaned until his knuckle nearly brushed a smudged cross. He pointed with a thumb that shook. "Men who left and never found the sea again," he muttered, the words so small I could have missed them if I hadn't been listening for anything that might stitch the rest of the night together.

Yusuf looked at the same blur and tapped the paper with a forefinger, as if feeling for the weakness of a seam. He folded the folio and slipped it under his arm like a thing to be guarded. "Keep it hidden—no curious eyes," he said, low enough that the map and the men and the sea between us could all be part of the same secret.

The wreck log lay beside the folio, folded smaller and worse for the sea. The diagram in it had been eaten by a torn edge; what was left looked like a hand that had tried to keep something from going away. Words bled at their margins; an attempt at a phrase had been scrubbed to a smudge and the paper had the desperate weight of a man who had run out of time.

They traded lines of talk over the two papers like sailors trading weather. "Reefs that move when you ain't looking. Lights that call a man off his course," someone said, and it was the sort of thing men said when they wanted to make danger sound less like fate and more like a mistake you could plan for.

Rasim's cough came again, harder this time. He reached for the coin I'd handed him and it slipped from his fingers, clicking once on the deck and skittering toward the hatch. Yusuf's boot caught it with a practised sweep; I caught Rasim's hand and dropped the bitter herb bundle into it. The smallness of it—two coins, a bundle of herbs, a steadying palm—was more expensive than any loud speech.

I felt the amulet at my throat prickle, a small and accurate pain. The world had rules I did not want broken; the amulet's law made them very clear. I answered without theatrics. "Azraq can fasten the council to my throat," I said, "but he cannot fasten my crew to the deck. That's mine to keep."

We prepared in the way that keeps a ship alive: the canvas rolled and lashed, lanterns trimmed so they would not gutter, a rope checked with a sailor's thumb. I gave a nod to Yusuf—firm, quick—and he looked at me the way a man looks at another when an oath is being kept between them. The Qitaf did what ships do when their captain decides a course: she learned her lines and braced herself.

I folded my hands on the rail and watched the city go thin as a moth's wing. "We would leave at dawn," I told the men, the plan small and sharp. Yusuf slipped the folio beneath his jacket and went to the binnacle to check the compasses; he moved like a man with a secret and a duty both. I told the men to stand ready to cast off.

A gull called once and the sound stole the last of the market's noise from my ears. The map was tucked, the stores stowed, and the men moved into the small, stubborn rituals that keep a ship together. When I walked the deck for the last check, my thumb brushed the amulet and the glass under it felt like a cold eye. I gave the word to stand by. It was a simple order. It was the one that would let us stop being talk and be a ship again.

## The prose

We left at first light, when the city still smelled of embers and the gulls were too hungry to mind a shipful of men. The Qitaf made herself small and quick in the grey—canvas trimmed, lines belled, the kind of movement that looks like a prayer said without words. I cut the last rope with a knife that felt like a promise and the harbor drew itself out of our wake behind a slow, indifferent tide.

Yusuf held the folio like a talisman under his coat, fingers worrying the edge as if he could smooth certainty into it. He did not say the word 'Jarrah' aloud, but he said it in the way a man can when he lays a course: in the angle of his head, in the steadiness of his hands. Rasim leaned at the wheel and coughed into the back of his sleeve the way a man keeps a small worry to himself. The cough left him thinner somehow, like one of the sleepier lanterns we had drawn down for the trip.

The men were quiet in the first hours; nervousness travels on a ship like a scent. It was not the loud sound of fear—there was no shouting, no prayer-chant—but the small trades and jokes missing from the deck, the way nets were checked twice, the way a knife gleamed where yesterday it would have sat dull. They listened when Yusuf spoke of bearings, and they listened harder when he tapped the folio's smudged coastlines. A smudge had become a thinned scar on the map; fingers had worn confidence away until only a suggestion of land remained. "Keep it close," Yusuf muttered to me once, not the same phrase as before but the same meaning: keep the folio, keep the map of our lives.

There was a man at the rail—one I had not seen well in the market—but I knew his sort: the sort that hears the sea and counts it. He pointed at a stain on the folio with a thumb that trembled. "Men who left and never found the sea again," he said. His voice was small enough for the gulls to take, but big enough to settle on the deck like a stone. The words slid between men like a current; you could see the thought spread, a cautious lowering of shoulders and a holding of hands closer to belt and knife.

Azraq stood aft with the ease of something that does not have to pretend to belong. He had not fussed with our ropes or our jests; he barely watched the crew at all. His silver eyes were where he kept his watch—sometimes they skimmed the horizon like a man looking for a shore, sometimes they looked inward, as if he felt the ship's bones. He watched the sea as if he'd placed a small moon over the deck and let it hang there, light enough to show but too cold to comfort. When I caught his gaze, I felt the amulet at my throat answer him the way a bell answers a hammer: a thin, precise thrum that ran like a wire from skin to bone.

The amulet pricked me, not with a fury but with the patient insistence of a thing doing what it was made to do. It was a reminder and a law—my throat remembered it even when my head tried to forget. I could have made a show of pulling at it, of twisting free; I did not. There were reasons for it beyond the council's patience and my stubbornness. I had my men to think of, and making a scene would have been the sort of thing that cost a crew its nerve.

Azraq did not hold a device or point to the sky; there was no magic machine worked into our rigging. How he watched was a detail the quarterdeck could not explain: he simply watched. It turned the men quiet in a different way, like a weather change that presses the air flat. "He watches like a moon," Rasim muttered once, half to himself, and the men laughed with a sound that was less than a laugh—a venting of breath that was as much to release a held thought as to make a joke.

Hours slipped. We ate small things under the boom—flat bread, an onion softened by stove smoke—and the work took rhythm again. The sea was close and honest, all folds and small mercies; the sky was a wash of grey that promised nothing if you asked it for a straight answer. Yusuf steered sometimes, checked the makeshift compass against his memory, and folded the folio into a pocket like someone closing a thin coffin. He did not show weakness. I liked that about him: a man who carries terror quietly is a better helmsman than one who shouts it.

They traded lines of talk over the folio and the wreck log like sailors trading weather.

As noon spread across the water the fog began to show like breath on the edge of a hand. It came slow and polite at first, a gauze that blurred the world's hard lines, then deeper, holding promises and closing off explanations. Men went quiet again. The Qitaf slowed because the sea made her now with less appetite for racing; the sea took itself seriously when the fog came.

They said the island's name then, but not as a map's point—more as a thing that could hang in the air and wait. It moved along the deck like a rag passed between hands. One of the younger lads, someone who had not yet learned to hide the taste of fear behind a grin, let it slip out. "Jarrah," he said, the consonants light and dangerous. The word found others like a tradesman's cry; it sounded in the mouth and then lived between breaths.

There was a long moment where the name and the fog were the same thing—unseen but obvious. I watched the line where sea met mist and felt my hands want to be elsewhere: on the charts, on the compass, on a man's shoulder. That want was straightforward. Command is always a thing of hands and small fixes.

We had to do two things as the island closed in: keep the Qitaf seaworthy, and keep my crew whole in their heads. The two tasks are the same sometimes. I kept my orders short, my steps efficient. When a shout came I answered it in less than a breath; when Yusuf folded the folio under his jacket I made him meet my eye and gave him a nod that meant, simply: keep it hidden.

At dusk the fog took the world and the world took on a narrower shape. Out of it a dark crop rose like a hand's shadow: the island's headland, not yet a shape but a promise of a shape. We did not call it out; we did not need to. "Jarrah," someone breathed, and the name seemed to be the first honest thing since dawn.

I felt the amulet thrum again then, a reminder tied to the silver of Azraq's eyes and the Council behind him. I felt the weight of a promise I had not chosen and the weight of the promises I had chosen—a crew, a ship, a way of keeping men alive. We were in the fog and nearer to the thing that would bind our hands as much as the amulet could. The island gave no mercy for being right.

I stood on the quarterdeck and watched the hand that was Jarrah draw itself out of the grey, every cove and inlet a small algebra of hazard. There was a work ahead that would ask me a debt. For now, the sea took us forward and the amulet sat cold at my throat and kept time with Azraq's moon.

## The prose

The sea did something you could feel in your teeth before it gave you a sight to match it: a fold that was not a wave so much as a hinge in the water, a quick, obscene doubling where the Qitaf's bow met a second skin of sea and the two moved for a breath as if to replace one another. I had felt enough wrong seas to name this one by the set of small betrayals it kept—light gone a degree ahead of us, a swell that smelled of old oil—but the way the world folded stopped me in my work.

The compass needle spent a breath where it had been still, then trembled and wandered like a thirsty thing. Binnacle glass went white and then clear as if someone had exhaled between us and the world. The chronometer on the rail juddered; its second hand missed, caught, and then stuttered on as if time itself had hiccuped. These were not the polite errors of weather to be calmed with a rope and patience; they looked like the sea making a decision.

Yusuf kept his thumb on the folio when the instruments betrayed us, as if touching paper could anchor a needle. He did not open it at first—he would not let the map speak while the deck was noisy with broken things—but when he did, the smudged crosses fell under our course like a second chart: the little dark Xs lined where the sea folded, exactly where my hands felt the deck dip. I did not read the map as new; I read my own memory against it, and the remembered lines in the wreck log that had no proper words left but a torn diagram in my head. The jagged fold in the water matched the torn diagram I'd smoothed from the wreck log.

Azraq watched from aft as if a pale, patient eye hung where the rigging met the fog, sweeping the horizon with a glance that made the deck feel measured. When he looked my way the amulet at my throat answered: a thin, precise thrum, the sort that sat under the skin and made the bone remember. It had the quality of law: quiet, implacable, and not mine. The thrum did not dictate sail trim, but it counted the cost of a choice the way a ledger counts coin.

Rasim's cough cut into the moment like a small bell. He held the wheel with both hands until the veins stood in them; the cough took a bit more from him each time and left him paler around the mouth. He tried to laugh it off, but the sound came out thin. "Keep her head to the swell," I told him, not because the compass said so but because the swell could be listened to with the body. He wheezed, coughed, bent his head back and took the order, one more thin man following a thin order on a narrower deck.

The crew moved with a single, urgent economy. Men re-tied lines with fingers that smelled of tar and fear; a pair shifted a coil of chain so we rode a half degree to starboard; someone lashed a canvas that had started to flog. I eased a sheet, then another, and told Yusuf to watch the folio but not to speak its crosses aloud. "Not here," I said—my voice had to be a task—and he folded the paper like a thing that might be carried into a grave. "Pull left on my call," I told Rasim, and when the sea folded again I felt the Qitaf answer through her timbers.

The reckoning was one of hands, not of instruments. The chronometer stuttered twice more and then kept time doggedly; the binnacle fogged and cleared; the needle spun a many-pointed hesitation. We compensated with the only things that had never failed us: sail trim, weight, and the small human measures of seamanship. I eased the sheet, shifted a coil of chain to starboard, and told Rasim to steer to the swell with his ear more than his eye.

It felt like reading a body. The Qitaf answered the weight and the cloth and the placement of crew like a patient horse. Yusuf kept his thumb along the folio's gutter as if it were a rosary, and in the quiet between the folds I heard the wreck-log memory kick at the back of my skull—no words, only shapes: the jag of a diagram, the suggestion that the island did not merely lie where the map pointed but made the sea do its lying for it. I had no right to make the wreck man's scrawl into a law, but the fold was a proof that did not need ink.

The folio itself felt like a body that had been handled too much. Pencil lines softened to scrawl; smudges had turned decisive marks into blind gestures. The marginal Xs, dark and blurred, were like teeth marks on a shore I had not seen in living memory; where they clustered the water felt heavy and cold under our feet. Yusuf traced one with his finger and flinched like a man touching a scar. "They mark the falls," he said, and then corrected himself into silence. Whether he meant the charts or the wreck nobody could tell, and that was all right. Not everything needed naming for us to act.

Azraq's eyes moved with the ease of something that had no need to pretend—an appraisal that did not seek our consent and did not ask for it. The amulet thumped when he tilted his head; I felt it in the hollow of my throat the way one feels a far drumbeat. It made the choice sharper: obey, bargain, break—none of them costless. For now my choice was immediate and small: keep the ship, keep the men, keep a map folded under a coat.

Rasim coughed again as we came through a shallow curl and his breath came out like a small surrender. I thought of the Qitaf as a single thing we all lent ourselves to—its hull and our habits braided—because the instruments had become unreliable and our bodies were the only machine left wholly our own. The men worked with hands that knew their jobs better than their mouths, a tight, moving thing that kept the Qitaf a single body.

Then, a hand's-breadth of wood—salt-soft, heat-scrambled, flecked with old black tar—bobbled against our hull and scraped past. It spun away with the haze and vanished as if swallowed by the same fold that had flipped the sea. For a moment no one spoke; the sight of flotsam is a small, private argument with the world. My throat tightened. The map had the crosses; the wreck had its half-diagram; the instruments had their sudden forgettings; and a piece of wood, carried by whatever made the sea fold, came close enough to touch.

I told Rasim to keep steering by the sound of the swell. "Watch for anything else," I said to Yusuf. The amulet at my throat kept its quiet time; Azraq's eye did not break its sweep. The island was near enough now that the fog tasted of it, a metallic salt that could have been anything—iron, old promises, the witches' loom. We had been delivered moments enough to choose which debts to spend.
